ety.text: From Middle English separaten (“to separate”), from separat (“separated”) + -en, from Latin sēparātus, perfect passive participle of sēparō (“to separate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from sē- (“apart”) + parō (“prepare”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“produce, procure, bring forward, bring forth”). Displaced Middle English scheden, from Old English scēadan (whence English shed). Doublet of sever, also derived from the same Latin verb.
From Middle English separat, see -ate (“adjective-forming suffix”) and Etymology 1 for more.
From a substantivization of the above adjective, see -ate (“noun-forming suffix”) and Etymology 1 for more.

senses.d: To divide (a thing) into separate parts.
ex: Separate the articles from the headings.

senses.d: To disunite from a group or mass; to disconnect.
ex: Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?
From the fine gold I separate the allay [alloy].

senses.d: To cause (things or people) to be separate.
ex: If the kids get too noisy, separate them for a few minutes.

senses.d: To divide itself into separate pieces or substances.
ex: The sauce will separate if you don't keep stirring.

senses.d: To set apart; to select from among others, as for a special use or service.
ex: Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them.

senses.d: Apart from (the rest); not connected to or attached to (anything else).
ex: This chair can be disassembled into five separate pieces.

senses.d: Not together (with); not united (to).
ex: I try to keep my personal life separate from work.

senses.d: Anything that is sold by itself, especially articles of clothing such as blouses, skirts, jackets, and pants.
ex: French taffeta evening separates – a puffball skirt, and a ruffled blouse – were pressed flat to drag them up to date.

senses.d: A printing of an article from a periodical as its own distinct publication and distributed independently, often with different page numbers.

ety.text: Probably borrowed from Latin sēparāre. Doublet of the inherited severare, older form of sceverare; compare also disceverare.
Borrowed from Latin dīvidere (“to divide, to separate”).

es:separar.gl: to separate, to detach (to disunite from a group or mass; to disconnect)

ety.text: A corruption of sect, influenced by Latin saeptum (“fence, enclosure”).

senses.d: A clan, tribe, or family, proceeding from a common progenitor; especially, one of the ancient clans of Ireland.
ex: The chief, struck by the illustration, asked at once to be baptized, and all his sept followed his example.

senses.d: An enclosure; a railing.

ety.text: Attested in the 15th Century C.E.; from Middle English separacioun, from Old French separacion, from Latin separatio, separationem. Morphologically separate + -ion.

senses.d: The act of disuniting two or more things, or the condition of being separated.
The act or condition of two or more people being separated from one another.
ex: […] my longing for her was undiminished despite our months of near-complete separation.

senses.d: The act or condition of a married couple living in separate homes while remaining legally married.
ex: […] she [knows] her great-aunt’s concern over her son Warren, his two divorces, and now Alice’s bitter separation from her husband, Ben.

senses.d: An agreement legalizing such an arrangement.
The place at which a division occurs.
An interval, gap or space that separates things or people.
An object that separates two spaces.
Departure from active duty, while not necessarily leaving the service entirely.
